title: What If You Never Cleaned Your House Again? (V2: photo What If)
sources: University of Kentucky Entomology, Fruit Flies (Ent-621): females lay about 500 eggs; egg to adult takes about a week; eggs laid on the surface of fermenting foods or other moist organic material; they also breed in drains, garbage disposals, trash containers, mops and rags; https://entomology.mgcafe.uky.edu/ef621

Iowa State University Extension, Yard and Garden, Moth fly (drain fly): usually originate in sink, bathtub, shower or floor drains, especially slow-running or seldom-used ones; larvae feed on the gelatinous film (slime) that builds up inside drains; https://yardandgarden.extension.iastate.edu/encyclopedia/moth-fly

University of Kentucky Entomology, Cockroach Control Manual (Ent-614): clean up spills and food waste, do not leave dirty dishes or pet food out overnight, do not let garbage pile up; up to 40 nymphs emerge from each German cockroach egg case; the German cockroach can produce several thousand offspring in less than a year; https://entomology.mgcafe.uky.edu/ef614

University of Kentucky Entomology, House Dust Mites (Ent-646): primary food is dander (skin scales) shed by people and pets; thousands of mites in a single gram of house dust are not uncommon; an infested mattress can contain millions; https://entomology.mgcafe.uky.edu/ef646

University of Kentucky Entomology, Carpet Beetles (Ent-601): carpet beetles thrive on lint, hair and debris under baseboards and in vents and ducts; a favored food of the larvae is dead insects; https://entomology.mgcafe.uky.edu/ef601

Penn State Extension, House Centipedes: feed on silverfish, firebrats, carpet beetle larvae, cockroaches, spiders and other small arthropods; frequent sightings indicate some prey arthropod is in abundance; https://extension.psu.edu/house-centipedes

Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station, House Centipede fact sheet: 15 pairs of legs (thirty legs); hunts cockroach nymphs, flies, silverfish and spiders; https://portal.ct.gov/-/media/caes/documents/publications/fact_sheets/entomology/house_centipede_scutigera.pdf
Timeline framing: the DAY numbers are a what-if story, not measured timelines; each day only uses a rate the sources give (egg to adult in about a week; thousands of roaches in less than a year).

beats.say: What if you never cleaned your house again?
Day one. You leave one dish in the sink, and a banana on the counter.
Fruit flies find it first. They lay eggs on the rotting fruit.
One female can lay about five hundred eggs.
Day three. You hear buzzing in the bathroom.
Drain flies. Their babies live in the slime inside your drain, and eat it.
You never scrub it, so the slime keeps feeding them.
Day seven. A fruit fly grows from egg to adult in about a week.
Then, silence. Something moves under the fridge.
Cockroaches. Your spills and crumbs are dinner.
One German cockroach egg case hatches up to forty babies.
Day thirty. Dust, hair and dead skin pile up in your bed.

beats.say: Dust mites eat the skin you shed. Thousands can live in one gram of dust.

shots.obs: wm:CSIRO ScienceImage 11085 A scanning electron micrograph of a female dust mite.jpg

beats.say: Carpet beetles move in for the lint, the hair, and the dead bugs.
Be honest. What would you do?

shots.obs: wm:Old table in a messy room (Unsplash).jpg

beats.say: Day three sixty five. One cockroach can lead to thousands in under a year.
Then something with thirty legs comes for them.
House centipedes. They hunt your cockroaches, spiders and beetle larvae.
The twist? Lots of centipedes means lots of bugs for them to eat.
So how many days would you last?
Follow me. Part two: never wash your sheets.
